flaw.ctx: You asked for a tolerant parser.
flaw.answer: The try/catch wraps the **whole loop**, so the first bad line ends parsing. Every good line after it is dropped, silently, with no count and no reason. 4 lines with the 2nd bad → 1 parsed.
flaw.fix: Per-line result with a reason (EventParser), counted; never a blanket catch.

qa.a: O(1) average for lookup, insert, remove; O(n) worst case if many keys collide. Enumeration is O(n) and order is not guaranteed.

Separate chaining, but without node objects: an `int[] buckets` of indices into an `Entry[]` array, each entry carrying its hash, key, value and a `next` index. Colliding keys form a chain through `next`.

When the entries array is full it grows to a larger prime (about double) and every entry is rehashed into new buckets — O(n) for that insert, amortised O(1). Pre-size with the constructor capacity when you know n.
Removing does not shrink anything: freed slots go on a free list for reuse. `TrimExcess()` shrinks. A struct key that is large is copied into every entry.

Most operators (`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`) are deferred: nothing runs until enumeration. `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Count()`, `First`, `Sum` execute immediately. `OrderBy` is deferred but buffers everything when enumerated.
The whole pipeline runs twice — including any I/O behind the source. Materialise once with `ToList()` if you need it twice.
An enumerator per operator, plus delegate and closure allocations for captured variables. Negligible for setup code, measurable in a per-request hot path.

qa.q: When is an explicit loop better?
qa.a: Hot paths, early exit with complex state, mutating as you go, or when you need to state complexity exactly — R5 hid an O(n log n) sort per call inside one readable line.

qa.q: Does async create a new thread?
qa.a: No. `async` lets a method be suspended; `await` on an incomplete task returns to the caller and schedules the rest as a continuation. No thread exists for the waiting.

The OS completes the I/O (I/O completion ports on Windows, epoll on Linux) and the continuation is queued to the thread pool or the captured context. The thread was free the whole time — that is the point.

Cooperatively. You pass a `CancellationToken` down; APIs that accept it observe it and throw `OperationCanceledException`. Nothing is aborted from outside. Blocked primitives need a registration to wake them (BoundedBlockingQueue does this).

qa.q: Can you await inside a lock?
qa.a: No — the compiler forbids it, because the continuation may run on another thread. Use `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync` with `Release` in a `finally` (R12 is what happens without the finally).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Read JSON-like event records, one per line, build typed objects, aggregate per action, and handle malformed input without losing the rest of the batch.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Typed model classes built from scratch
- Per action: count, mean and max latency, distinct users
- Malformed lines counted by reason, never thrown
- Streams: holds aggregates, not the input

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Bad input is data. The design question is the **error model**: a result type with a reason, counted per reason, so a million-line batch with three bad rows produces a million-minus-three results and an explanation — not an exception, and not a silent drop.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: `Event` record; `ParseResult` with `Reject?` reason; `EventParser.Parse` returning a result; `Aggregator.Consume(IEnumerable<string>)` holding only per-action accumulators.

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Per line: parse JSON → must be an object → each field present and correctly typed → range checks → Event.
- Accumulate per action; summary sorted by count, then name.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Type | Why |
|---|---|
| record Event | Immutable, value equality, one line to declare |
| enum Reject | Enumerable reasons → countable, testable |
| JsonDocument | Parses without binding, so type errors are per field and reportable |
| HashSet<string> per action | Distinct users — the one part that grows |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
- Per line: parse JSON → must be an object → each field present and correctly typed → range checks → Event.
- Accumulate per action; summary sorted by count, then name.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md: O(lines). Memory O(actions + distinct users per action).

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
- Ten lines: four good, one of each reject reason, one blank → accepted 4, each reason counted once.
- view: count 3, mean 200, max 300, 2 distinct users.

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- This is where to delegate most: "Write record types and a JsonDocument-based parser for this schema, returning a result with a Reject reason instead of throwing."
- Then audit the error handling line by line — that is what is being scored.
- Ask it for malformed test lines, one per reason.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe a result type with a reject reason per line — never an exception — so one malformed record cannot abort the batch, and an aggregator that holds only per-action accumulators while streaming. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Consume, if the input is split across threads concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- A try/catch around the whole loop: the first bad line silently drops every line after it (R7).
- `int.Parse` on a JSON number that is a float or too large.
- Deserialising straight into the model: one bad field throws for the whole record with no reason.
- Mean computed in int — integer division.

**Verification exercise:** Edge case / silent data loss — The try/catch wraps the **whole loop**, so the first bad line ends parsing. Every good line after it is dropped, silently, with no count and no reason. 4 lines with the 2nd bad → 1 parsed.

learn.title: 13 · Concurrency considerations
learn.md:
Parallel aggregation should not share accumulators; give each worker its own and merge at the end — no locks on the hot path.

**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *Make it thread-safe / parallel.* — Per-worker accumulators, merge at the end — no shared lock

learn.title: 14 · Scalability considerations
learn.md:
**Level 4 — Scale**

- *The JSON is 1 GB. Can we avoid loading it?* — Line-by-line streaming; for one big array, Utf8JsonReader
- *Distinct users at scale.* — HyperLogLog, ~1–2% error

learn.title: 15 · Production considerations
learn.md:
- Emit reject counts as metrics; alert on a reject-rate jump (a schema change upstream).
- Keep a sample of rejected lines for debugging, with PII redaction.

**Level 5 — Productionisation**

- *What do you monitor?* — Reject rate by reason
- *Upstream changes the schema.* — Reject spike alert; tolerant reader for additive changes

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
- *Parse and aggregate.* — Model, parser, aggregator — three small types.
- *Malformed input.* — Result type; count per reason; keep going.
- *A 50 GB file.* — Already streaming. Distinct users becomes a HyperLogLog sketch; say the error (~1–2%).
- *Parallelise.* — Partition lines, aggregate per partition, merge accumulators (counts and sums add; max takes max; sets union / HLL merge).
- *Late or duplicate events.* — Idempotency by event id; windowing by event time with a lateness bound.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Missing fields, wrong types, nested objects, an empty file?* — Result type with a reason per line; empty → empty summary

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Time and memory?* — O(lines); O(actions + distinct users)
- *What if N is very large?* — Already streaming

stages.name: Parse, model, aggregate
stages.yours: Model first: `Event(User, Action, Ts, Ms)` and the `Reject` reasons. The rule: **a bad line is counted under exactly one reason and never stops the batch**. Write five bad lines, one per reason, and three good ones.
stages.ai: **Co-generate** the parser: System.Text.Json plumbing is boilerplate. The reasons and the accumulator are yours.
bad: Parse these JSON lines and aggregate by action, skipping bad lines.
A `try/catch` around the **whole loop** — the first bad line ends parsing — or a catch-all that skips silently with no count.
"Skipping" hides data loss: nothing counted, nothing reported
No reasons, so you cannot test each one
good: Write Aggregator.Consume(IEnumerable<string> lines): parse each line with System.Text.Json. Skip blank lines. Count each bad line in Rejected under exactly one Reject reason: NotJson, NotAnObject, MissingField, WrongType (user/action not a non-empty string; ts/ms not an integer), OutOfRange (ms < 0). One bad line must never stop the rest. Per action keep count, sum and max of ms, and distinct users. Summary sorted by count desc then action (ordinal); mean as a double. Keep my Event record and Reject enum. Show only Aggregator.
stages.reply: Typical defect (verified planted flaw R7): **try/catch around the whole loop** — 4 lines with the 2nd bad → 1 parsed, silently.
validate: One line per reason — each counted once, under the right reason
A bad line in the middle: lines after it still counted
stages.fix: Whole-loop try/catch → **a narrow follow-up**: "Move the try/catch inside the loop so each line is handled on its own; count the failure under NotJson and continue."
stages.say: "A bad line is data, not an exception. One malformed record must not lose the next million."
stages.require: Implement `Aggregator.Consume` and `Summary`. Count each rejected line under exactly one `Reject` reason; never throw on bad input.
stages.say_iv: Here is a log of JSON-like events, one per line. Build the classes, and give me per-action counts and latency stats. Some lines are garbage.

stages.name: The file is 1 GB
stages.yours: Say the constraint: **one pass over an IEnumerable, aggregates only**. Then say what still grows: the set of distinct users per action (→ a HyperLogLog sketch at scale).
stages.ai: **AI reviews** — ask for a memory review, not new code.
bad: Make it handle a 1 GB file.
`File.ReadAllLines` "to load it efficiently", or `lines.ToList()` so it can count first — the whole file in memory.
It optimises the wrong thing (speed of loading, not memory)
good: Review Consume for memory on a 1 GB input. It must enumerate the lines exactly once and keep only per-action aggregates. List everything that grows with the input, most significant first. Do not rewrite the code. The Aggregator is pasted below. No ToList, no ReadAllLines. Explain why each item grows. Keep my code as it is.
**"Do not rewrite"** keeps it a review
stages.reply: A good reply names the per-action HashSet of users as the only thing that grows. A bad one suggests `.ToList()` or a `.Count()` before the loop — a second enumeration.
validate: Enumerated exactly once — count enumerations in the test
Only aggregates kept; distinct users is the one growing set
stages.say: "One pass, aggregates only. The only thing that grows is distinct users — at scale that becomes a HyperLogLog sketch, about 1.6% error in 12 KB."
stages.require: `Consume` must enumerate its input exactly once and must not buffer it. The test streams 300,000 generated lines through an enumerable that throws if read twice.
stages.say_iv: What happens if the input is a 1 GB file? Can you process it without loading everything into memory?
